title: Magnetostatics
description: Magnetic forces, Biot–Savart and Ampère's law for wires, coils and cables, and magnetic flux.

study.title: Lorentz force
study.body: A charge moving with velocity $\mathbf{v}$ feels $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$, perpendicular to both $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ (right-hand rule, reversed for negative $q$). Because it is always perpendicular to the motion it does **no work**: it bends the path but never changes the speed. In a uniform $B$ a charge moving perpendicular to it circles with radius $r = mv/|q|B$.

study.title: Force on currents
study.body: A straight wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$ in a uniform field feels $\mathbf{F} = I\mathbf{L}\times\mathbf{B}$, magnitude $BIL\sin\theta$. Two long parallel wires a distance $d$ apart **attract** when their currents flow the same way and **repel** when opposite. The force per metre is below.

study.title: Biot–Savart law
study.body: Each current element $I\,d\mathbf{l}$ adds a field perpendicular to $d\mathbf{l}$ and to the line to the observation point, falling as $1/R^2$; $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ H/m. Results to remember: a straight segment at distance $\rho$, whose ends are seen under angles $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ from the perpendicular (second line; an infinite wire has $\alpha = \pm90°$, giving $\mu_0I/2\pi\rho$), and the centre of a circular loop (third line).

study.title: Ampère's law
study.body: The circulation of $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{B}/\mu_0$ around a closed path equals the current through it (right-hand rule for the direction). With a circle around a long wire, $H\cdot2\pi\rho = I$. Inside a solid round wire of radius $a$ only the fraction $\rho^2/a^2$ of the current is enclosed, so $B$ grows linearly and peaks at the surface.
study.formula: \begin{array}{c} \displaystyle \oint_C \mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{enc} \\[0.5em] \displaystyle B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi\rho} \quad (\rho \ge a) \\[0.5em] \displaystyle B = \frac{\mu_0 I\rho}{2\pi a^2} \quad (\rho \le a) \end{array}

study.title: Coax, solenoid and toroid
study.body:
**Coax** (inner radius $a$, outer conductor $b$ to $c$, currents $\pm I$): $B$ rises inside the inner conductor, is $\mu_0I/2\pi\rho$ in the insulator, falls to zero through the outer conductor and is **zero outside** (enclosed current 0).
**Long solenoid** ($n = N/\ell$ turns per metre): uniform $B = \mu_0nI$ inside, about zero outside. **Toroid**: $B = \mu_0NI/2\pi\rho$ inside the core, zero outside.

study.title: Magnetic flux and Gauss's law for B
study.body: The magnetic flux through a surface is $\Phi = \int\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ in webers (Wb = T·m²); for a flat area in a uniform field $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ with $\theta$ the angle between $\mathbf{B}$ and the normal. There are no magnetic monopoles: field lines close on themselves, so the net flux out of **any closed** surface is zero.

steps.title: The Lorentz force
steps.body: A charge $q$ moving with velocity $\mathbf{v}$ through a magnetic flux density $\mathbf{B}$ (in tesla, T) feels a force perpendicular to both. Use the right-hand rule for $\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ and flip it for negative charges. Together with the electric force this is the **Lorentz force**.

steps.prompt: A proton moves in the $+y$ direction through a uniform field $\mathbf{B}$ in the $+z$ direction. Which way is the magnetic force on it?
steps.explanation: $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B} \propto \hat{y}\times\hat{z} = \hat{x}$, and $q > 0$, so the force is along $+x$. It is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, never along them. An electron would be pushed along $-x$.

steps.prompt: A straight wire of length {{L*100}} cm carries {{I|A}} in a uniform field of {{B|T}}. The wire makes an angle of {{th}}° with the field. Find the magnitude of the force on it.
steps.explanation: $F = BIL\sin\theta$ = {{B}} T × {{I}} A × {{L}} m × sin {{th}}° = {{I*L*B*sin(rad(th))|N}}. Only the part of the wire perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$ feels a force.

steps.title: Biot–Savart law
steps.body: Every small piece of current $I\,d\mathbf{l}$ creates a magnetic field that circles around it and falls off as $1/R^2$. Adding (integrating) all the pieces gives the field of any current path. At the centre of a circular loop of radius $a$ all pieces add in the same direction (perpendicular to the loop), giving the result below; $N$ turns give $N$ times as much.

steps.prompt: A flat circular coil of {{N}} turn(s) with radius {{a*100}} cm carries {{I|A}}. Find $B$ at its centre.
steps.explanation: $B = \frac{\mu_0NI}{2a}$ = 4π×10⁻⁷ × {{N}} × {{I}} / (2 × {{a}}) = {{mu0*N*I/(2*a)|T}}. Note $2a$, not $2\pi a$ (that would be the long-wire formula).

steps.title: Ampère's law
steps.body: With symmetry, Ampère's law is much quicker than Biot–Savart: the circulation of $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{B}/\mu_0$ around a closed path equals the current enclosed. Around a long straight wire $\mathbf{H}$ circles the wire (right-hand rule: thumb along $I$, fingers along $\mathbf{H}$) and is constant on a circle of radius $\rho$.

steps.prompt: Find $B$ at {{r*100}} cm from a long straight wire carrying {{I|A}}.
steps.explanation: $B = \frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi\rho}$ = 4π×10⁻⁷ × {{I}} / (2π × {{r}}) = 2×10⁻⁷ × {{I}} / {{r}} = {{mu0*I/(2*pi*r)|T}}. (For comparison, the Earth's field is about 50 µT.)

steps.title: Try it: inside and outside a wire
steps.body: A solid round wire of radius $a$ carries $I$ spread evenly over its cross-section. Inside, Ampère's loop of radius $\rho$ encloses only $I\rho^2/a^2$, so $B$ grows linearly; outside it falls as $1/\rho$. Drag $a$: the field outside (readout at 10 mm) does not change, only the peak at the surface does. Drag $I$: everything scales with the current.
steps.formula: \begin{array}{c} \displaystyle B = \frac{\mu_0 I\rho}{2\pi a^2} \quad (\rho \le a) \\[0.5em] \displaystyle B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi\rho} \quad (\rho \ge a) \end{array}

steps.prompt: A long wire along the $z$ axis carries current in the $+z$ direction. Which way does $\mathbf{B}$ point at a point on the positive $x$ axis?
steps.explanation: Thumb along $+z$, fingers curl counter-clockwise seen from above: $\mathbf{B}$ is along $\hat{\phi}$. On the $+x$ axis $\hat{\phi} = +\hat{y}$. Magnetic field lines of a wire are circles around it, never radial or along the wire.

steps.prompt: A static magnetic field can speed up a charged particle.
steps.explanation: False. The magnetic force $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ is always perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$, so it does no work ($\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0$). It changes the direction of motion, not the speed. Particle accelerators use **electric** fields to add energy and magnetic fields to steer.

steps.prompt: Match each current configuration to the field it produces.
steps.explanation: The wire, solenoid and toroid follow from Ampère's law (circle, rectangle, circle inside the core). The loop centre needs Biot–Savart, since a single loop has too little symmetry for Ampère's law.

steps.prompt: A long solenoid has {{N}} turns over a length of {{l*100}} cm and carries {{I|A}}. Find $B$ inside it, away from the ends.
steps.explanation: Ampère's law around a rectangle with one side inside: $H\ell = NI$. So $B = \mu_0\frac{N}{\ell}I$ = 4π×10⁻⁷ × {{N}} / {{l}} × {{I}} = {{mu0*N*I/l|T}}. It does not depend on the radius of the solenoid.

steps.prompt: A toroid with {{N}} turns carries {{I|A}}. Find $B$ inside the core at {{r*100}} cm from the toroid's axis.
steps.explanation: A circle of radius $\rho$ inside the core encloses the current $NI$ (every turn passes through it once): $H\cdot2\pi\rho = NI$. $B = \frac{\mu_0NI}{2\pi\rho}$ = 4π×10⁻⁷ × {{N}} × {{I}} / (2π × {{r}}) = {{mu0*N*I/(2*pi*r)|T}}.

steps.prompt: Two long parallel wires {{d*1000}} mm apart carry {{I1|A}} and {{I2|A}} in **opposite** directions. Find the magnitude of the force on {{L}} m of either wire.
steps.explanation:
Wire 1 creates $B = \mu_0I_1/2\pi d$ at wire 2, and wire 2 feels $F = BI_2L$:
$F = \frac{\mu_0I_1I_2L}{2\pi d}$ = 2×10⁻⁷ × {{I1}} × {{I2}} × {{L}} / {{d}} = {{mu0*I1*I2*L/(2*pi*d)|N}}. Opposite currents **repel**.

steps.prompt: An electron moves at {{v/1e6}}×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform field of {{B|T}}.

ask.prompt: Find the radius of its circular path, in mm.
ask.explanation: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $|q|vB = mv^2/r$, so $r = \frac{mv}{|q|B}$ = 9.109×10⁻³¹ × {{v/1e6}}×10⁶ / (1.602×10⁻¹⁹ × {{B}}) = {{1000*me*v/(qe*B)}} mm.

ask.prompt: Find the time for one revolution.
ask.explanation: $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}$ = 2π × 9.109×10⁻³¹ / (1.602×10⁻¹⁹ × {{B}}) = {{2*pi*me/(qe*B)|s}}. The speed cancels: faster electrons make bigger circles in the same time (the cyclotron period).

steps.prompt: A straight wire segment of length {{L*100}} cm carries {{I|A}}. Find $B$ at a point {{r*100}} cm from the segment's midpoint, on its perpendicular bisector.
steps.explanation:
Biot–Savart for a segment: $B = \frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi\rho}(\sin\alpha_2 - \sin\alpha_1)$ with $\sin\alpha_2 = -\sin\alpha_1 = \frac{L/2}{\sqrt{\rho^2+L^2/4}}$ = {{(L/2)/sqrt(r^2+L^2/4)}}.
$B$ = 10⁻⁷ × {{I}} / {{r}} × 2 × {{(L/2)/sqrt(r^2+L^2/4)}} = {{mu0*I*L/(4*pi*r*sqrt(r^2+L^2/4))|T}}. An infinite wire would give {{mu0*I/(2*pi*r)|T}}.

steps.prompt: A long solid round wire of radius {{a*1000}} mm carries {{I|A}}, spread uniformly over its cross-section.

ask.prompt: Find $B$ at {{ri*1000}} mm from the axis (inside the wire).
ask.explanation: A circle of radius $\rho < a$ encloses $I\rho^2/a^2$ = {{I*f^2}} A. $H\cdot2\pi\rho = I\rho^2/a^2$, so $B = \frac{\mu_0I\rho}{2\pi a^2}$ = 2×10⁻⁷ × {{I}} × {{ri}} / {{a^2}} = {{mu0*I*ri/(2*pi*a^2)|T}}.

ask.prompt: Find $B$ at {{ro*1000}} mm from the axis.
ask.explanation: Outside the wire the whole current is enclosed: $B = \frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi\rho}$ = 2×10⁻⁷ × {{I}} / {{ro}} = {{mu0*I/(2*pi*ro)|T}}.

steps.prompt: A flat loop of area {{A*1e4}} cm² sits in a uniform field of {{B|T}}. The angle between $\mathbf{B}$ and the loop's **normal** is {{th}}°. Find the magnetic flux through the loop.
steps.explanation: $\Phi = \mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{S} = BA\cos\theta$ = {{B}} T × {{A}} m² × cos {{th}}° = {{B*A*cos(rad(th))|Wb}}. The flux is largest when $\mathbf{B}$ is along the normal (perpendicular to the loop's plane) and zero when $\mathbf{B}$ lies in the plane.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the measured flux density $B$ versus distance $\rho$ from a long straight wire. Find the current in the wire.
steps.explanation: The marked point is at $\rho$ = {{r1*1000}} mm with $B$ = {{B1|T}}. From $B = \frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi\rho}$: $I = \frac{2\pi\rho B}{\mu_0}$ = {{r1}} × {{B1}} / 2×10⁻⁷ = {{I|A}}. Any point on the curve gives the same $I$, since $B\rho$ is constant.

steps.prompt: The net magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero, even if the surface surrounds one pole of a bar magnet.
steps.explanation: True: $\oint\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0$ ($\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$). Field lines leaving the north pole outside the magnet return through the inside of the magnet, so every line that leaves the surface also enters it. There are no isolated magnetic charges.

steps.prompt: A coaxial cable has an inner conductor of radius {{a*1000}} mm and an outer conductor from {{b*1000}} mm to {{c*1000}} mm. It carries {{I|A}} out along the inner conductor and back along the outer one.

ask.prompt: Find $B$ at {{r1*1000}} mm from the axis.
ask.explanation: {{r1*1000}} mm lies in the insulator, so a circle there encloses only the inner current $I$: $B = \frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi\rho}$ = 2×10⁻⁷ × {{I}} / {{r1}} = {{mu0*I/(2*pi*r1)|T}}.

ask.prompt: Find $B$ at {{r2*1000}} mm from the axis.
ask.explanation:
{{r2*1000}} mm is inside the outer conductor. The circle encloses $I$ minus the part of the return current inside it: $I_{enc} = I\left(1 - \frac{\rho^2-b^2}{c^2-b^2}\right) = I\frac{c^2-\rho^2}{c^2-b^2}$ = {{I*(c^2-r2^2)/(c^2-b^2)|A}}.
$B = \frac{\mu_0I_{enc}}{2\pi\rho}$ = {{mu0*I/(2*pi*r2)*(c^2-r2^2)/(c^2-b^2)|T}}.

ask.prompt: Find $B$ at {{(c+1e-3)*1000}} mm from the axis.
ask.explanation: Outside the cable a circle encloses $I - I = 0$, so $B = 0$. That is why coax does not radiate a magnetic field and is not disturbed by nearby wiring.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows $B(\rho)$ for a coaxial cable (inner conductor radius $a$ = 1, outer conductor from $b$ = 2 to $c$ = 2.5) carrying equal and opposite currents?
steps.explanation: Inside the inner conductor $B \propto \rho$ (enclosed current $\propto \rho^2$). In the insulator $B = \mu_0I/2\pi\rho$. Through the outer conductor the enclosed current falls **gradually** from $I$ to 0, so $B$ falls smoothly to zero at $c$, and outside $B = 0$. The curve that keeps going as $1/\rho$ ignores the return current; the one that drops at $b$ treats the outer conductor as infinitely thin.

steps.prompt: A rectangular loop lies in the same plane as a long straight wire carrying {{I|A}}. Its sides of length {{h*100}} cm run parallel to the wire, at distances {{d*100}} cm and {{(d+w)*100}} cm from it. Find the magnetic flux through the loop.
steps.explanation: $B = \mu_0I/2\pi\rho$ varies across the loop, so integrate strips of width $d\rho$ and length $h$: $\Phi = \int_d^{d+w}\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi\rho}h\,d\rho = \frac{\mu_0Ih}{2\pi}\ln\frac{d+w}{d}$ = 2×10⁻⁷ × {{I}} × {{h}} × ln({{(d+w)/d}}) = {{mu0*I*h/(2*pi)*ln((d+w)/d)|Wb}}.

steps.prompt: A square loop with sides of {{s*100}} cm carries {{I|A}}. Find $B$ at its centre.
steps.explanation:
Each side is a segment at distance $s/2$ from the centre, seen under $\alpha = \pm45°$: $B_{side} = \frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi(s/2)}(\sin45° + \sin45°) = \frac{\sqrt2\mu_0I}{2\pi s}$. All four sides add in the same direction:
$B = \frac{2\sqrt2\mu_0I}{\pi s}$ = {{2*sqrt(2)*mu0*I/(pi*s)|T}}. (A circular loop of radius $s/2$ would give {{mu0*I/s|T}}.)

steps.prompt: A long wire carries $I_1$ = {{I1|A}}. A rectangular loop in the same plane carries $I_2$ = {{I2|A}}; its two sides of length {{h*100}} cm are parallel to the wire at {{d*100}} cm and {{(d+w)*100}} cm, and on the near side $I_2$ flows in the same direction as $I_1$. Find the magnitude of the net force on the loop.
steps.explanation: Near side (parallel currents): attraction $\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2h}{2\pi d}$ = {{mu0*I1*I2*h/(2*pi*d)|N}}. Far side (opposite current): repulsion $\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2h}{2\pi(d+w)}$ = {{mu0*I1*I2*h/(2*pi*(d+w))|N}}. The forces on the two perpendicular sides cancel. Net: {{mu0*I1*I2*h/(2*pi)*(1/d - 1/(d+w))|N}} **towards** the wire.

steps.prompt: Two long parallel wires are {{d*100}} cm apart and carry {{I1|A}} and {{I2|A}}. Find $B$ midway between them.

ask.explanation: Each wire is $d/2$ from the midpoint and gives $\mu_0I/2\pi(d/2) = \mu_0I/\pi d$. With opposite currents both fields point the same way between the wires (right-hand rule), so they add: $B = \frac{\mu_0(I_1+I_2)}{\pi d}$ = {{mu0*(I1+I2)/(pi*d)|T}}.

ask.prompt: The currents flow in the **same** direction.
ask.explanation: Each wire gives $\mu_0I/\pi d$ at the midpoint, but with parallel currents the two fields point in **opposite** directions between the wires and subtract: $B = \frac{\mu_0|I_1-I_2|}{\pi d}$ = {{mu0*abs(I1-I2)/(pi*d)|T}}.

steps.prompt: A circular loop of radius {{a*100}} cm carries {{I|A}}. Find $B$ on its axis at {{z*100}} cm from the centre.
steps.explanation:
Biot–Savart: every element is at distance $\sqrt{a^2+z^2}$; the components perpendicular to the axis cancel and the axial parts add:
$B = \frac{\mu_0Ia^2}{2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}}$ = {{mu0*I*a^2/(2*(a^2+z^2)^1.5)|T}}. At $z = 0$ this gives $\mu_0I/2a$ = {{mu0*I/(2*a)|T}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for finding $B$ with Ampère's law in order.
items: Use symmetry to find the direction of $\mathbf{H}$ and what it depends on
Choose a closed path along which $H$ is constant and tangent (or perpendicular)
Write the circulation as $H$ times the path length
Find the current enclosed by the path, with signs
steps.explanation: The same pattern as Gauss's law. Signs of the enclosed current follow the right-hand rule with the path direction; return currents (coax) subtract.
